meta.label: Washing machines
tradeoffLabels: lower energy and water use per wash
built and legally supported to last
meta.attribution: Covers washing machines placed on the EU market, plus three ways to do laundry without buying a new one. Energy and water figures come from each model's own EU Product Information Sheet, published in the European Product Registry for Energy Labelling (EPREL) under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2014. Every figure quoted is for the mandatory 'eco 40-60' programme, the single reference cycle EU law requires every washing machine to be tested and rated on, so the numbers are comparable across brands even though a household rarely runs that exact cycle. The environment score here is 100 minus the model's published Energy Efficiency Index (EEIW), so a lower index scores higher; the underlying kWh and litre figures are in each entry's own note. The longevity score comes from the same sheet's 'minimum duration of the guarantee offered by the supplier', converted to a 0-100 scale where 36 months would score 100. That figure sits on top of, not instead of, the two-year minimum consumer guarantee EU law provides on almost all goods sold in the EU regardless of what a supplier states on its own sheet. The durability score is France's mandatory durability index (indice de durabilite), which folds a repairability mark and a reliability mark into one score out of 10 and has applied to washing machines since April 2025; manufacturers publish the underlying filing on data.gouv.fr, the French government's open data platform, and this entry multiplies the published mark by ten. No EU-wide equivalent exists yet, so a durability score is only shown for models whose French filing could be matched to a specific machine, almost always by the identical model identifier on both registers, with any looser match (a market suffix or a naming difference) stated in that entry's note; it describes the France-market registration of what is usually the same engineering platform sold under the same or a near-identical model name elsewhere in the EU. Beko, Whirlpool, Indesit and Hotpoint are now common brands of Beko Europe, the joint venture Arcelik and Whirlpool formed in April 2024 and which Arcelik now owns outright; they are kept as separate entries here because they are still sold, priced and positioned as separate lines. Two retailer own labels, Electro Depot's Valberg and Currys' Logik, are included as budget floors. The launderette entry is sourced to a UK trade body and is marked UK rather than EU for that reason, though self-service laundries operate across Europe under other names. Suggest changes via Contribute.

products.name: Repairing the machine you have
products.description: Calling an independent repairer or a manufacturer service line instead of replacing the machine. EU law gives a repaired machine a long formal support tail: key spare parts must stay available for a decade, and repair information must reach professional repairers within two years of a model going on sale.

environment.note: The European Environment Agency reports that large household appliances, including washing machines, saw average lifespans rise 1.8 per cent a year from 11.6 years in 2019 to 12.5 years in 2023, and that extending product lifespans reduces the resource use, waste and emissions caused by replacing goods before they fail, though it also notes that 'replacement was preferred over repair, which was seen as too expensive' for large appliances.

longevity.note: Under EU Ecodesign Regulation 2019/2023, Annex II, manufacturers must make key spare parts, including the motor, drum, pumps, heating elements and circuit boards, available to professional repairers for 10 years after the last unit of a model is placed on the market, deliver ordered parts within 15 working days, and give professional repairers access to repair and diagnostic information from two years after a model's market placement.

accessibility.note: The same EU regulation requires repair and diagnostic information, including disassembly maps, wiring diagrams and fault codes, to reach professional repairers within two years of a model's market placement, which is what lets an independent repairer take on a job rather than only the manufacturer's own service network.

products.name: Secondhand and giveaway networks
products.brand: not a purchase, or a small one
products.description: Buying a used machine or taking one for free through a local giveaway network instead of buying new. Reuse avoids the resource and manufacturing footprint of a new appliance, at the cost of no manufacturer guarantee and no energy label for the specific unit.

environment.note: The European Environment Agency frames reuse and repair as ways to 'reduce the demand for new products', and states that premature disposal across the EU causes an estimated 261 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions, consumes 30 million tonnes of resources and generates 35 million tonnes of waste each year, impacts that keeping a machine in use through resale or reuse avoids.

accessibility.note: Freecycle's own about page says its network has 'spread to more than 110 countries' and operates in '32 countries including the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, The United States, and all European Union countries', where members post things they no longer want for anyone nearby to collect for free.

products.brand: not a purchase, pay per wash
products.description: Using a coin- or app-operated launderette instead of owning a machine at all. The only option in this roster that needs no purchase, no installation and no plumbing work, which matters most for renters without a hookup.

accessibility.note: NALI, the UK trade association for self-service launderettes, says they serve 'students, those in rented accommodation with no machine provided, people with little time or inclination to launder at home and the elderly or disabled who are unable to manage it', and are 'a welcome saviour when the domestic machine breaks down', without the user buying, installing or maintaining any equipment.
